curator.reply: The command card's interpretation is the slow part of the card, because every press is one model round trip. The app first builds a digest of the map: card names, kinds, one line about each and the wires, bounded so a large map cannot flood the prompt. It then sends that digest with the instruction verbatim and the whole act catalogue, and the model answers with either one fenced block of acts, one short clarifying question, or one sentence. The parsing is local and instant, so the wall-clock cost is essentially the provider's latency plus the time it takes to generate the block. In practice the generation matters: a short block is fast, a long one is not, and a model that thinks before answering adds its reasoning time on top. Because the digest is bounded and the catalogue is fixed, the prompt size is roughly constant regardless of how big the map is, which means a huge map does not make the call much slower. The acts themselves are instant: they are proposals, filed as ghosts, and nothing is written until the person accepts the script. If the instruction is ambiguous the model is asked to ask one question rather than guess, which is another round trip but a shorter one. This measurement is a single pass on one provider and one model, so it may not reflect a different provider, a different model, or a loaded network.
